bib.title: Compacter: Efficient Low-Rank Hypercomplex Adapter Layers

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "COMPACTER: Efficient Low-Rank Hypercomplex Adapter Layers", Rabeeh Karimi Mahabadi, James Henderson, Sebastian Ruder. NeurIPS 2021 (arXiv:2106.04647v2, 27 Nov 2021). File: /Users/ramsey-wise/workspace/learn-ai-engineering/ai-engineering/08-multimodal-engineering/sources/mahabadi-2021-compacter.pdf

COVERAGE: I read all 67,195 of 67,195 chars, covering the body, Tables 1-11 and Appendices A-E. I skimmed the references only for where the method comes from. Nothing was skipped.

**Most important for the note: the paper never compares against LoRA.** LoRA (Hu et al.) is not among the baselines and is not cited. The closest baseline is "ADAPTER-LOWRANK", which is a bottleneck adapter whose weights are each a product of two rank-one weights. That is not LoRA. Any LoRA comparison in "Which layers you reached" cannot be sourced to this paper.

CLAIMS
- claim: Compacter++ trains 0.047% of T5-base's parameters and matches full fine-tuning on GLUE.
  number: 0.047%; GLUE avg 86.47 vs 86.50 for full fine-tuning
  setup: T5-base (222M), GLUE, output layer frozen, layer norms trained, n=4. Best hyperparameters picked on validation.
  quote: "By only training0.047% of a pretrained model's parameters,COMPACTER performs on par with standard ﬁne-tuning on GLUE"; Table 1: "T5BASE 8.0×1 100% ... 86.50" / "COMPACTER ++ (n = 4) 1.002 0.047% ... 86.47"
  where: abstract p1; Table 1 p7

- claim: Compacter (an adapter after both attention and FFN) trains 0.073% and slightly beats full fine-tuning on the GLUE average.
  number: 0.073%, 86.62 vs 86.50
  setup: T5-base, GLUE, n=4
  quote: "COMPACTER (n = 4) 1.004 0.073% 63.75 93.00 ... 77.70 86.62"
  where: Table 1 p7

- claim: Main GLUE comparison against other parameter-efficient methods (avg score, % trained per task).
  number: Adapter 0.832%/85.78; Pfeiffer-Adapter 0.427%/86.32; AdapterDrop 0.494%/85.85; Adapter-LowRank 0.073%/85.82; Prompt tuning-T 0.034%/75.95; Intrinsic-SAID 0.009%/85.45; BitFit 0.126%/84.97
  setup: T5-base, GLUE, output layer frozen for all methods
  quote: "ADAPTER 1.065 0.832% ... 85.78"; "BITFIT 1.010 0.126% ... 84.97"; "PFEIFFER -A DAPTER 1.032 0.427% ... 86.32"
  where: Table 1 p7

- claim: On SuperGLUE, Compacter and Compacter++ beat full fine-tuning and the other parameter-efficient methods.
  number: Compacter++ 0.048%/71.82; Compacter 0.073%/71.57; T5-base 70.06; Adapter 70.55; BitFit 67.30
  setup: T5-base, SuperGLUE, n=12. Small test sets: half of the validation set was used for tasks under 10k samples.
  quote: "COMPACTER ++ (n = 12) 1.002 0.048% ... 71.82"; "T5BASE 6.0×1 100% ... 70.06"
  where: Table 2 p8

- claim: Memory and time cost for one MNLI epoch (Table 3). Compacter++ cuts memory by 41.94% and time by 26.51% against full fine-tuning. BitFit is the cheapest on both but loses accuracy.
  number: T5-base 167.99 MB / 42.13 min; Compacter++ 118.35 MB (-41.94%) / 30.96 min (-26.51%); Compacter 123.91 (-35.57%) / 36.48 (-13.41%); Adapter 124.02 (-35.45%) / 31.81 (-24.50%); BitFit 102.31 (-64.20%) / 27.36 (-35.06%); Prompt tuning +24.42% memory; Intrinsic-SAID +41.14% memory, +241.82% time
  setup: 1 epoch of MNLI. For each method, the largest batch that fits a 24 GB budget. Adapter size 24, n=4, 100 prefix tokens. RTX 3090. The "MB" units are as printed. They look odd next to a 24 GB budget, so treat them as relative values.
  quote: "For each method, we select the largest batch size that ﬁts a ﬁxed budget of the GPU memory (24 GB)"; "COMPACTER ++ 0.047% 118.35 -41.94% 30.96 -26.51%"; "BITFIT, by not storing intermediate activations, has the lowest memory requirement (-64.2% relative to T5BASE) and is the fastest (-35.06% relative to T5BASE) at the cost of lower quantitative performance (1.53 points lower; see Table 1)"
  where: §5.5 p8-9; Table 3 p9

- claim: Training very few parameters does not by itself save memory. Prompt tuning and Intrinsic-SAID train the fewest parameters, yet they use more memory and train more slowly than full fine-tuning.
  number: 41.14% and 24.42% extra memory
  setup: same as Table 3
  quote: "they both come with high memory overhead (41.14% and 24.42% relative to full ﬁne-tuning (T5BASE) respectively), are slowest to train"
  where: p9

- claim: Parameter complexity. A standard adapter costs O(kd) per layer and Compacter costs O(k+d). Total parameters: adapters 2L(2kd), PHM-adapter 4L(kd/n + n^3), Compacter 4L(k+d)+n^3.
  number: "2127.66× fewer parameters than standard ﬁne-tuning"
  setup: analytic. The 2127.66× figure is for T5-base.
  quote: "the total number of parameters ofCOMPACTER is 4L(k+d)+n3 for a transformer withL layers in the encoder and decoder"; "despite learning 2127.66× fewer parameters than standard ﬁne-tuning"
  where: §4 p5; conclusion p10

- claim: Compared with a standard adapter, Compacter is 11.4× smaller, Compacter++ 17.7× smaller and PHM-Adapter 4.64× smaller.
  number: 11.4×, 17.7×, 4.64×
  setup: T5-base. Parameter counts are reported for d=24.
  quote: "a parameter reduction at a remarkable rate of 11.4×. COMPACTER ++ even reduces the parameters further by 17.7× in total"; "PHM-A DAPTER reduces the parameters ofADAPTER from 0.83% to 0.179% (withn = 12), being 4.64× more parameter-efﬁcient"
  where: App. B p16; p8

- claim: At Compacter's scale, layer norms and biases make up most of what is trained, so the trainable count barely changes with n.
  number: Compacter: LN 28.49% and biases 23.51% of its trainable params. Compacter++: 44.01% and 18.15%. PHM-Adapter: 8.63% and 7.12%.
  setup: T5-base, n=4
  quote: "forn = 4, for COMPACTER with 0.073% of trainable parameters, LN and B make up 28.49% and 23.51% respectively of its trainable parameters; for COMPACTER ++ with 0.047% of trainable parameters, LN and B make up 44.01% and 18.15%"
  where: App. B p16

- claim: The output layer holds 11.1% of T5-base's parameters, so tuning it swamps the PEFT savings. Every method then lands near 11.1-11.9%. Compacter++ scores about the same with the output layer tuned or frozen.
  number: 11.1%; Adapter 85.78 rises to 86.48 when the output layer is tuned; Compacter++ (n=4) 86.55 at 11.11%
  quote: "the output layer includes 11.1% of the parameters of T5 BASE"; "not ﬁne-tuning the classiﬁer hurts the performance substantially (85.78 versus 86.48; cf. Appendix C)"; "COMPACTER ++ (n = 4) 1.002 11.11% ... 86.55"
  where: fn5 p6; p7; Table 7 p17

- claim: Where the adapter is placed matters. Dropping adapters from the lower layers (AdapterDrop) hurts, and keeping only one adapter per block works.
  number: AdapterDrop -0.65 avg (85.85)
  setup: T5-base GLUE, adapters dropped from the first 5 encoder and decoder layers
  quote: "ADAPTER DROP obtains lower performance than ﬁne-tuning, demonstrating that adapting the lower layers of an encoder-decoder T5 model is important for its performance"; "ADAPTER DROP obtains a lower performance (-0.65 less on average across all tasks.)"
  where: p7, p9

- claim: With small data, Compacter++ beats full fine-tuning.
  number: subsets of 100-4000 samples, 5 seeds (exact values appear only in Fig. 4)
  setup: GLUE subsampled to {100,500,1000,2000,4000} samples, trained for 1000/200/100/50/25 epochs, GTX 1080 Ti, batch 40
  quote: "We show mean and standard deviation across 5 seeds."; "COMPACTER ++ substantially improves the results in the low-resource setting"
  where: Fig. 4 p10; App. A p15

- claim: On the smaller T5-small (60M), every parameter-efficient method falls below full fine-tuning.
  number: T5-small 82.71; Adapter 0.698%/81.06; Compacter (n=8) 0.091%/80.97; BitFit 0.190%/78.90
  quote: "All parameter-efﬁcient ﬁne-tuning methods are performing worse than full ﬁne-tuning with this small model size."
  where: App. E p18, Table 9

- claim: Prompt tuning is unstable and lags far behind. BitFit also trails, especially on low-resource tasks.
  number: Prompt tuning-R GLUE avg 71.49, with CoLA at 0.47 marked "best of 6 seeds"
  quote: "due to insatiability during training, we restarted experiments with 6 random seeds and report the best"
  where: Table 1 caption p7

LIMITS
- No LoRA baseline. BitFit was re-implemented by the authors on T5, with biases re-introduced.
- Variance: the main tables (1, 2, 6-9) report single runs, using the best validation checkpoint and hyperparameters, with no error bars. Only Fig. 4 has mean and std over 5 seeds. Unstable baselines are reported as best-of-6 seeds. Several T5-small runs "were not successful" across seeds.
- Small test sets. For tasks under 10k samples, half of the original validation set is the test set. Gaps of tenths of a point (86.47 vs 86.50) fall within noise.
- Scale: T5-base and T5-small only. "Due to the huge computational costs of training these models, we could not run experiments on such a large scale" (T5-large/3B/11B).
- NLP text-to-text only, with no vision or VLM experiments. Transfer to VLMs is an inference the note would be making, not something the paper shows.
- The efficiency figures come from a single epoch on MNLI with adapter size 24. The memory units are oddly small for a 24 GB budget.
- Dated: these are 2021 encoder-decoder baselines from before LoRA and QLoRA became standard.
- Future work the authors name: removing biases and layer norms, and combining with AdapterDrop.

BUILDS ON
- Adapters: Houlsby et al., ICML 2019 [1]; Rebuffi et al., CVPR 2018 [15]
- PHM layers: Zhang et al., ICLR 2021 [17] (PyTorch implementation by Le et al., ICANN 2021 [29])
- Low-rank / intrinsic dimension: Li et al., ICLR 2018 [13]; Aghajanyan et al., ACL 2021 [14]
- Baselines: Pfeiffer et al. (AdapterFusion) EACL 2021 [31]; Rücklé et al. (AdapterDrop) EMNLP 2021 [23]; Lester et al. EMNLP 2021 [12]; Li and Liang 2021 [10]; Cai et al. (TinyTL) NeurIPS 2020 [33]; Ravfogel et al. (BitFit) arXiv 2106.10199 [34]
- Slow/fast weights: Wen et al. (BatchEnsemble) ICLR 2020 [25]
- Frozen output layer: Mahabadi et al. ACL 2021 [30]
- Model: T5, Raffel et al. JMLR 2020 [3]

CODE: No code listing. The paper links https://github.com/rabeehk/compacter. Key equations, verbatim:
- Adapter (Eq. 2, p3): "Al(x) =Ul(GeLU(Dl(x)))+x"
- LPHM (Eq. 5, p4): "W = n∑ i=1 Ai⊗Bi = n∑ i=1 Ai⊗(sit⊤i )". In words: Ai is n×n and shared across all layers, and si,ti are rank-one factors specific to each layer (r=1 by default).
- Hyperparameters (App. A, p15): AdamW, LR swept over 3e-5 to 3e-1. Compacter uses 3e-3, while full FT, Adapter and BitFit use 3e-4. GLUE: max length 128, batch 100, 500 warm-up steps.

FIGURES
- Fig. 1 (p2): "The average score on GLUE (y axis), percentage of trainable parameters per task (x axis, in log scale), and memory footprint (size of the circles) of different methods." One picture shows the three-way trade-off between parameters, score and memory.
- Fig. 2 (p2): adapter placement after attention and FFN, with only adapters and layer norms trained. A direct visual for "which layers you reached".
- Fig. 3 (p4): how shared Ai and per-layer rank-one Bi build each layer's weights. Faster than reading the algebra.
- Fig. 4 (p10): low-resource curves with mean and std over 5 seeds.

PROBLEMS: Extraction was clean overall. Some sub- and superscripts are garbled (for example "kn× dn" for k/n × d/n, and "n4" for n^4), and some words run together. The Table 1 caption says "insatiability", which is a typo in the source for "instability". The numeric values of Fig. 4 are not in the text. There were no embedded instructions.
